candidate_targets: those struggling with loss of purpose or will to live
contraindications: May be less effective for individuals unable to identify any personal values or connections
original_extraction.evidence_text:
If you want a better job, that’s a goal. Once you’ve got it: goal achieved. But if you want to apply
yourself fully at work, to be attentive to detail, supportive to your colleagues and engaged in what
you're doing, those are values.

---

Auschwitz was the most notorious of the Nazi death camps. We can scarcely begin to imagine what
took place there: the horrific abuse and torture, the extremes of human degradation, the countless
deaths through disease, violence, starvation and the infamous mass gas chambers. Viktor Frankl
was a Jewish psychiatrist who survived years of unspeakable horror in Auschwitz and other camps,
which he described in gruesome detail in his awe-inspiring book Man’s Search for Meaning.

---

One of the most fascinating revelations in this book is that, contrary to what you would expect, the
people who survived longest in the death camps were often not the physically fittest and strongest,
but rather, those who were most connected with a purpose in life. If prisoners could connect with
something they valued, such as a loving relationship with their children or an important book they
wished to write, that connection gave them something to live for; something that made it
worthwhile to endure all that suffering. Those who could not connect with a deeper value soon lost
the will to live—and thus, their lives.

---

Frankl’s own sense of purpose came from several sources. For example, he deeply valued his loving
relationship with his wife and was determined to survive so he could one day see her again. Many a
time during strenuous work shifts in the snow, with his feet in agony from frostbite and his body
racked with pain from brutal beatings, he would conjure up a mental image of his wife and think
about how much he loved her. That sense of connection was enough to keep him going.
generation_rules: Identify and clarify personal values distinct from goals
Encourage mental visualization of valued relationships or purposes
pause_rules: Pause after introducing key concepts such as values versus goals
Pause to allow reflection on personal meaningful connections
original_extraction.psychological_function: Supporting survival and endurance through meaningful engagement with valued relationships or goals
repetition_rules: Reinforce distinction between goals and values
Repeat connection between values and survival or endurance
original_extraction.therapeutic_function: Enhancing connection to personal values to foster resilience and purpose in life
voice_rules: Use empathetic and hopeful tone when discussing values and purpose
Present examples of resilience grounded in values
